title: Zero-Clustering Geometry in Realistic Fractional Quantum Hall Wave Functions
authors: Xin Wan, Ziang Wang, Zi-Xiang Hu, Zhao Liu
abstract: The clustering pattern of zeros in the ground state of a fractional quantum Hall system is a defining feature of its topological properties. We analyze the geometrical fluctuations of the zeros around individual electrons and propose to use the displacement ratio of the zeros to visualize and measure the distance of a realistic state to a model wave function. The distribution of the zero displacement ratio behaves like an order parameter in the transition from a Laughlin phase to a topologically trivial one. The statistical comparison between quantum Hall states belonging to different Jain sequences leads to a composite fermion fluid description of the $ν= 1/5$ ground state with long-range Coulomb interaction that agrees almost perfectly for as few as $3$-$5$ electrons, overcoming the long-standing difficulties of accommodating the competing liquid and crystal orders at short distances.
summary: This work develops the zero displacement ratio ($\zeta$) as a quantitative diagnostic tool to map out phase transitions in Fractional Quantum Hall systems by analyzing the geometry of wave function zeros. By comparing results from Laughlin models against realistic Coulomb interactions, the authors show that the zero structure collapses or shifts predictably when topological order is lost. The findings strongly support Composite Fermion descriptions over simpler crystal approximations for describing these correlated electron liquids.
main_problem: The study aims to quantify how deviations from ideal model wave functions affect the topological properties of Fractional Quantum Hall (FQH) systems, particularly during phase transitions.
main_result:
The zero displacement ratio ($\zeta$) serves as a diagnostic tool: its statistical behavior reveals the transition from Laughlin liquid order to charge-ordered or crystalline phases. Furthermore, Composite Fermion Fluid descriptions provide an improved description of $
u=1/5$ states compared to simple crystal embeddings.
method: The analysis relies on calculating and analyzing the geometric distribution (density maps) of zeros in the ground state wave functions using a zero displacement ratio ($\zeta$) derived from nearest neighbor zeros. Overlap amplitudes are also used to compare different theoretical approximations.
model_or_system:
The system is strongly interacting electrons confined to the Lowest Landau Level, modeled at fractional fillings like $
u=1/3$ and $
u=1/5$. The Hamiltonian is varied by mixing terms between simple pseudopotentials ($V_1$) and full Coulomb interactions ($H_C$).
key_observables: Zero displacement ratio ($\zeta$), density distribution $P(\phi)$ of the zero argument, Kurtosis ($K$) of this distribution, Overlap Amplitude ($O$), and Pair Correlation Function ($g(r, R)$).
important_parameters:
Filling fractions $
u=1/3$ and $
u=1/5$; mixing parameters ($\lambda$ or $\eta$); the ratio defining $\zeta$.
main_assumptions: The analysis often relies on studying specific small-N systems ($N=3$) to extract general scaling laws, and approximations are made when constructing Composite Fermion states.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the evolution of zero patterns (density maps) as interaction strength changes, showing shifts in $\zeta$ peaks. Other figures track order parameters like $P(\phi)$ and overlap amplitudes ($O$) versus tuning parameters ($\lambda$ or $\eta$).
paper_structure:
The paper systematically analyzes the geometry of zeros for different FQH states ($
u=1/3$, $
u=1/5$), introducing the zero displacement ratio as a diagnostic. It then compares results from idealized Laughlin models against realistic Coulomb interactions, culminating in the development and testing of Composite Fermion Fluid descriptions.
why_interesting: The use of geometric properties (zero clustering) to diagnose topological order is a powerful, non-local probe that complements standard energy gap or correlation function measurements. This methodology could be adapted to study other exotic quantum phases where local observables are insufficient.
